characters: Nelson Forson: a 14-year-old school-magazine reporter, with a recorder and a notebook, in a school uniform.
Madam Janet Sakyi: a conservationist from an environmental group, in field clothes, with a map of a forest and rivers.
Victor Ennin: a 17-year-old young man who has worked in small-scale mining, in work clothes and boots, with a tired, honest face.
Mr Oscar Awuah: a district official, in a shirt and tie, with a folder; and an elderly paramount chief, seen from a distance, in traditional cloth.

narrationPlan.voice: Thoughtful boy’s voice for Nelson; distinct, respectful adult voices for each interviewee
narrationPlan.pace: Careful and balanced, like a good interview (about 118 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: Soft forest sounds with a thoughtful guitar; a clear, steady tune at the conclusion (placeholder)
culturalNotes: Nelson, Madam Sakyi, Victor, Mr Awuah and Mrs Ahiable are invented. The Atewa Range Forest Reserve is real and the debate is real, so the story attributes each claim by role and does not name any politician or company. No claim in the story should be taught as settled fact.

Facts from published sources: conservation groups say Atewa holds the headwaters of the Ayensu, Densu and Birim rivers, which supply more than five million people; Global Wildlife Conservation reports about 3,000 plant species and over 570 butterfly species; in September 2026 environmental groups said illegal mining had spread into the reserve and called for a national park; they estimate eco-tourism and agroforestry could bring over US$5 million a year and at least 3,000 jobs; the paramount chief of the area has been reported to oppose bauxite mining; the government has argued that bauxite mining could bring revenue and that new technology could limit damage.

Formal commercial bauxite mining remains contested and, as far as the writer knows, the reserve has not been upgraded to a national park, while illegal mining is reported as an active threat; in September 2026 the Forestry Commission and the national anti-illegal mining team (NAIMOS, Operation Green Shield) were reported to have made arrests; the operation was announced on 22 October 2026 and some reports say three suspects were arrested at its launch. On 2 November 2026 Adom reported an armed clash during the operation in the reserve (one suspected miner killed, four arrested); this is deliberately kept out of the story. These details may have changed; teachers should check recent news before use.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
Check the current status of the Atewa bauxite plans and of illegal mining in the reserve with up-to-date news and official statements, and correct the story if it has changed.
Check every attributed claim, especially the five-million-people figure, the species counts and the tourism and jobs estimates, against the original reports.
Check that the story is balanced and that Victor is presented with dignity and not as a villain; ask a local youth-programme worker to review.

teacherGuide.overview: A story about a real, contested question: should a water-source forest be mined or protected? It teaches how to separate claims from facts, listen to every side and write a discursive essay.
learningGoals: Explain why a forest at a river’s headwaters matters.
List the claims of each side and say who made them.
Write a discursive essay with a reasoned conclusion.
beforeReading: Ask: what would make you change your mind on a hard question?
whileReading: At page 6, ask learners to sort the claims into “estimates”, “claims” and “facts that can be checked”.
afterReading: Write a discursive essay on a local land-use question, naming the owner of each claim.
Hold a role-play town meeting with the four voices, respectfully.
discussion: Who should decide on mining in a forest reserve, and how?
How can young people like Victor find safe, fair work?
reflection: What would you want to learn before deciding on a question like this when you are a leader?

support: Provide an essay frame: On the one hand… On the other hand… However… In conclusion…
stretch: Write a formal letter to a district official asking for the latest information on a forest near you, with two reasons.

localiseThis: Use a real local forest or water source; check the latest news; invite community members to speak.

factCheck.claim: Conservation groups say Atewa holds the headwaters of three rivers (the Ayensu, Densu and Birim) that supply more than five million people; reports cite about 3,000 plant species and over 570 butterfly species; the paramount chief has been reported to oppose bauxite mining; the government has argued that bauxite mining could bring revenue and that new technology could limit damage.
factCheck.explanation: These are attributed claims from advocacy groups, news reports and an environmental news site; the figures are not independently verified here and the status of the plans may have changed.
factCheck.reference: GhanaWeb (14 September 2026) report on a joint statement by environmental groups; MyJoyOnline (2019) on conservation groups’ campaign; Afrik21 on Atewa and bauxite. Verify against current sources.
